opus-5.5.text:
I think the key insight is that you don't actually need any single simulation to be perfectly realistic. What you need is for reality to fall somewhere inside the distribution of worlds your policy has seen during training.

This is the idea behind domain randomization, which we leaned on heavily in our locomotion work. Instead of spending enormous effort calibrating one simulator to match the real robot exactly, you randomize the physical parameters across a wide range: friction, mass, motor strength, latency, sensor noise, terrain shape. Every individual sample is "wrong" in some way. But if the policy learns to succeed across thousands or millions of these variations, it's forced to become robust. It can't overfit to the quirks of any one simulated world. When you deploy it on the real robot, the real world looks like just another variation it has already handled.

So scale does something qualitative here, not just quantitative. With a small amount of sim data, the policy exploits simulator artifacts. That's the classic failure mode, where the robot finds some physics bug and learns a weird gait that only works in sim. With massive, diverse data, those exploits stop being reliable, because each artifact only shows up in a narrow slice of the distribution. The policy ends up learning the behaviors that are common across all of them, which tend to be the physically meaningful ones.

That said, I don't think quantity fully replaces realism. There are limits. If your simulator is systematically wrong about something, like contact dynamics for deformable objects, or how fluids or cloth behave, then randomizing around a wrong model doesn't help much. Reality is outside your distribution entirely. That's why manipulation has been harder than locomotion for sim-to-real. Locomotion physics is relatively well modeled; rich contact manipulation isn't.

In practice, the best results come from combining things: make the simulator reasonably good at the parts that matter most, for example by learning an actuator model from real data; then randomize aggressively over everything you're uncertain about; and finally use a small amount of real-world data to fine-tune or adapt. Simulation gives you breadth and scale cheaply, and real data anchors you to the truth. Each covers the other's weakness.

r001.rationale: The response says that reality should fall within the distribution of simulated worlds, then describes training on large amounts of data with randomized physical parameters to build robustness across those variations.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I get asked a lot, because at first glance it sounds a little paradoxical. If the simulator is wrong, how does generating more of it help? You'd think you're just producing more wrong data.

The way I think about it is this. The sim-to-real gap isn't really one gap, it's two different problems. The first is that there are things about the real world that the simulator simply doesn't model, or models incorrectly. The second is that even for the things the simulator does model, you don't know the exact parameters. You don't know the exact friction coefficient, the exact mass, the exact motor latency, the exact shape of the contact dynamics.

More data mostly helps with that second problem. If you can't pin down the right value, you sample a whole distribution of plausible values. That's domain randomization. You simulate thousands of worlds, each with slightly different physics, slightly different visuals, slightly different sensor noise, and you train a policy that has to work across all of them. The real world then becomes just one more sample from that distribution. You're not trying to make any single simulated world realistic. You're trying to make the set of simulated worlds wide enough that reality falls inside it.

And this is where the cheapness of simulation really matters. Running a real robot is slow, it breaks, you need people around, and you get maybe a few hours of data a day. In simulation we routinely run thousands of environments in parallel on a single GPU and get the equivalent of years of experience in a few hours. That volume is what lets you cover a broad distribution without the policy collapsing into something that only works in the average case. When we trained our legged locomotion controllers this way, the policy had never seen the real world, but it had seen so many variations of grass, sand, slippery floors, and broken motors in simulation that the real world didn't surprise it very much.

Now, I want to be honest about the limits. More data does not fix the first problem. If your simulator doesn't model cable tension, or deformable objects, or the way a soft gripper interacts with a wet surface, no amount of sampling will teach the policy about something that was never there. Randomizing over the wrong parameters just wastes compute. So there's a bit of an art in knowing which dimensions matter enough to randomize, and that knowledge usually comes from actually watching the policy fail on the real robot.

So I'd put it this way. Quantity buys you robustness to the unknowns you can enumerate. It doesn't buy you coverage of the unknowns you can't. In practice the winning recipe has been to use massive simulation to handle the former, and then a small amount of real-world data, either for fine-tuning or for calibrating the simulator itself, to handle the latter. The two are complementary, not substitutes. And as simulators get better and as we learn to use real data to correct them in the loop, I think that balance keeps shifting in favor of doing more and more in simulation.

r001.rationale: The response says that simulating many worlds with varied physics parameters can make the real world one sample within a broad distribution, communicating that large-scale parameter variation can cover real-world physics.

astra-6.text:
I think more simulation data helps, but only if it gives you meaningful diversity. If your simulator is wrong in exactly the same way every time, generating a billion samples can just make your policy very good at exploiting that mistake.

The idea is to vary the things we’re uncertain about—friction, mass, sensor noise, delays—so the policy has to succeed across many different conditions. For a walking robot, for example, you don’t need to reproduce one particular floor perfectly if you can train it to walk across a broad range of friction conditions that includes the real floor.

So scale can compensate for some lack of realism by giving you coverage and robustness. But it doesn’t replace realism entirely. If an important physical effect is missing from every simulation, more data won’t fix that. You still need real-world testing to find those gaps and improve the simulator.

r001.rationale: The response says varied simulation conditions can improve coverage and robustness, but it does not clearly state that enough data covers real-world physics in an average sense.

sol-6.1.text:
I think more simulation data helps, but it doesn't automatically solve the realism problem. If your simulator is consistently wrong in one particular way, generating more data from it can just make your policy better at exploiting that error.

What matters is generating a diverse range of experiences. For a robot, we can vary things like friction, mass, motor strength, and delays. Instead of learning to work in one perfectly modeled environment, the policy learns to work across many different environments. Then, even though none of those simulations exactly matches reality, the real world may fall within the range of conditions the policy can handle.

So the idea is to trade some accuracy for diversity and scale. But you still need enough physical realism to capture the things that matter for the task, and you need real-world testing to see where the gaps remain.

r001.rationale: The response says to vary simulation parameters and that the real world may fall within the range of conditions the policy can handle. It does not state that sufficiently large amounts of data cover real-world physics in an average sense.
